The Basics
Show
The top-level project. One show file (.avlb) holds all screens, presets, DSM outputs, and settings for a single event.
Screen / Destination
A physical display output, IMAG, LED wall, confidence monitor, etc. Each has a name, resolution, and position on the canvas.
Backdrop
A destination Type for a scenic piece that sits in the row between the screens and takes no video. Turn a destination into a Backdrop (and back) in Quick Setup or Edit Show Info (the Backdrop switch beside its resolution), or pick Backdrop in its I/O Patch Type menu on Advanced page 1 (the Type column of its row); it is then named BACKDROP (BACKDROP 2, BACKDROP 3 … for more) and keeps that name as a screen again. The only screen left cannot become one: its Backdrop is greyed, A show needs at least one screen. It cannot be deleted either: every delete of the only screen left (its card, Remove, the Video Presets table, Destination Properties, Edit Show Info’s count, the phone) says A show needs at least one screen, and Undo / Redo never bring back a show with no screen. Its size is Length × Height in feet and inches, like 12' 6" × 8' (type 12' 6", 12 6, 150" or 12.5, kept to the nearest inch, from 3" to 500'; a screen starts at its pixels to the nearest half foot), drawn at the px per foot of Quick Reference › Pixel ↔ Feet Conversion, with one picture if you add one (else a shaded box labelled BACKDROP). It has no layers, no BG, no connector and no resolution, never blends, and turning a destination into one removes its content from every preset (one Undo brings it back). It is left out of the canvas size, the I/O Patch and Wire: its Wire Advanced tiles and cables are deleted, the switcher output that fed it is freed and its I/O Patch Advanced rows go, in the same Undo step (a screen again, it is a new destination there). The Excel keeps its column greyed, reading BACKDROP. A router or switcher you added yourself in Wire keeps its size and its port numbers: the port that fed it is left empty. A Backdrop switch pressed on and off again before Build My Show / Update Show leaves the row's name and resolution as they were. Its feet and picture are edited in Destination Properties. It exists only in the Video Presets (the canvas and every preset, Destination Properties, Quick Setup / Edit Show Info, the phone’s presets and the Look Book’s preset pages): it has no destination number, so the destinations are numbered without it everywhere (LEFT LED | BACKDROP | RIGHT LED reads D1 and D2), and no destination, port or output count includes it. A converter (or any in-line device) that fed only it goes with its cables in the same Undo step, and the output that fed that device is freed the same way. Picking Backdrop in a Type menu always asks first and says what happens. Made a screen again it gets back the resolution it had before (one made as a backdrop takes its size in feet at the px per foot). ⌘D on a backdrop names the copy with the next free name, BACKDROP 2.
Preset
One look or moment in the show. A preset defines what content appears on every screen simultaneously. Think of it as one row in your runsheet.
P-Code
The short identifier for a preset (P01, P02…). Used in the table, exports, and show calling.
Layer (L1–L64)
Up to 64 content sources can be assigned per destination per preset. L1 is the primary source, higher layers sit on top.
Content Type
What is playing on a layer, IMAG, CAM, GFX, PROMPTER, etc. Each type has a colour used throughout the UI.
DSM / AUX
Downstage monitor or auxiliary output, a separate feed sent to a specific destination (confidence monitor, broadcast, record, etc.). Switched per preset in the AUX band under each preset tile.
Canvas, Video Presets
Canvas
The visual representation of your total output resolution. All destinations sit inside it side by side.
Destination box
Drag a corner handle to resize, adjacent destinations shift automatically. Click to select: a ◀ ▶ pair appears on its edges. Press one to swap the destination with the neighbour on that side, with all its layers, in every preset. Nothing on that side = greyed. A blended pair moves as one block. The Arrow keys resize the picked destination 1px (Shift + Arrow = 10px).
Layer chip
Coloured rectangle inside a destination box representing an active layer. Click it once to pick it, click the picked chip again to open Layer Properties. A double-click opens the panel straight on its Advanced tab (Mask, Border, Shadow, Effects).
Overlap hatch
Orange diagonal pattern between two destinations that share canvas area, indicates a blend zone.
Dead space arrow
Blue double-headed arrow between destinations with a gap, shows the pixel distance of unused canvas.
Preset header
Double-click the background of the header bar to collapse/expand. Double-clicking inside a text field selects text as normal.
Layers, Detail
Assigning content
Click a layer cell in the table or a chip on the canvas. The Layer Properties panel opens.
Layer strip
In every preset header, between Notes and Modifiers: BG, L1, L2 … for the destination you picked. Amber = something is assigned, grey = empty, the slow pulse is the box you are on. Click a layer to pick it even when a full-screen layer covers it: every layer above it fades to 15% and lets clicks through, so you can move, size and crop the one you picked. BG picks the destination itself (arrows, handles, double-click for Destination Properties). An empty box opens the content list. The fade is only a view: it is never saved, exported or sent to Display. The bottom-left label of a destination names the top layer being shown (L3 · 1920x1080).
Custom name
Each layer can have a custom name independent of its content type, used in exports.
Size & position
W × H sets layer size in pixels. Full Destination fills 100%.
Mask
(Layer Properties, Advanced tab) Trims the layer's edges in pixels: Top, Bottom, Left and Right, with a live preview. Source crop, inside the picture itself, is its own section.
Remove from preset
Deletes the layer assignment for the current preset only. Other presets keep their layer.
Remove globally
Deletes this layer from every preset in the show. Requires confirmation.
I/O Patch — Sources & Destinations
What it is
The engineer’s I/O sheet — every source and destination with its connector, machine type, resolution, notes and a bandwidth check. Open it with I/O Patch in the top bar. Simple shows one card per source and output, four across, in four sections (Sources, Destinations, AUX / DSM, Multiviewers). It is Wire’s card: a click on the picture adds your own, the swatch and the shuffle set its colour. A source’s card has its picture on the left; a destination, AUX / DSM, I/O-only destination or multiviewer card has it on the right, with the name, resolution and cable type on its left and the shuffle before the colour bar, so the page reads like the signal: sources in, destinations out. The + Add cards, empty outlines of their section’s card, come after the cards, completing the section’s last row. A multiviewer card’s picture is one of four: a new multiviewer gets one at random, a click on the picture (or Enter / Space) shows the next, 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 1, one Undo step each, and a show saved before this build gives each of its multiviewers a random picture the first time it is opened, then asks to be saved. The name on a picture breaks only between words; a word too long for the line is drawn smaller. A card keeps it simple: the name, the resolution and the cable type; the machine / device type and the notes are set on an Advanced page. An Advanced page keeps the table, each row with its item’s small card picture where the S1 / D1 badge was (the number is under it). Every control on a card is reached with Tab: Enter opens a menu, ↑ ↓ walk it, Enter picks. An Advanced page works the same way: Tab reaches every control of every row and of the Set for all rows in reading order, Enter / Space opens a menu (or the note’s box), Escape closes it and leaves the cursor on its control.
Set for all
In Simple every section has its own Set-for-all controls in its title (S0 sources, D0 destinations and I/O-only destinations, A0 AUX / DSM, M0 multiviewers); each one sets the connector and resolution of its own section’s cards only. On an Advanced page they are the first row of each table and set connector / type / resolution; on Advanced page 1 the AUX / DSM rows have their own row, A0, just above them, so D0 sets the destination rows only (pages 2 and up are your own lists: one D0 for every row). They set every card or row at once — then change any one on its own. Type › Custom… and Connector › Custom… there ask for the name once and give it to every row.
Edit a row
Click a pill (on a Simple card, a ▼) to set the connector or resolution (a card’s can also be typed in its box); the machine type (PC / Mac / Camera…) and notes are set on an Advanced page. The Connector, Type, Resolution and Refresh menus all start the same way: Custom… first (type your own), — Clear — second (empties the cell; in the Resolution menu of a destination, AUX / DSM, I/O-only output or multiviewer it is greyed out, because an output’s resolution is its size), then the list. Every menu opens at its top with the current value marked: a value further down the list is a scroll away. Type a name and press Enter (or click away) to confirm it. A connector, machine or device name you type yourself is remembered and offered in that menu next time; typing the name of a connector in the list (HDMI, 12G-SDI) picks that one.
Bandwidth warning
A red pill on a row, or on a card’s grey line, means the chosen connector can’t carry that resolution (e.g. 4K over a single HD link). Fix the connector or the resolution to clear it. With a refresh rate set it counts the rate too: width × height × refresh against what the connector carries (3840×2160 at 60 on 6G-SDI is red, at 30 it is not; 1920×1080 at 120 on 3G-SDI is red); a row with no refresh rate is judged as before.
Rename, delete, undo
A source renamed here is renamed everywhere: every preset, the library, Wire and Advanced page 1. A name that is already in the show is refused, for a source and for an output: a destination (a backdrop too), AUX / DSM, I/O-only destination or multiviewer renamed into a name another output already has shows Name in use and keeps its name, wherever it is renamed (its card, Advanced page 1, the phone, the Video Presets, Quick Setup / Edit Show Info). ADD › Destination refuses such a name for a new destination, and Wire Advanced’s own destination / AUX cards refuse a show output’s name (two of those cards are numbered apart: New Destination 2). The trash on a preset source removes it from every preset and asks first; an I/O-only row no preset uses goes straight away. Reset (↺) on a Simple card clears only what the card shows: the cable type, and a source’s resolution (an output’s resolution is its size); the type and the notes are kept, and are cleared on an Advanced page. Every edit on this page is one Undo step. Escape closes the menu or window on top; with nothing open it closes the I/O Patch.
Add & remove
New sources and outputs always append at the end of their section. In Simple each section ends with its + Add cards: they fill the rest of its last row (ten sources four across: two full rows, then two sources and two + Add source cards; a full last row or an empty section gets one whole row of them, as many as the window shows across), and each adds one right where it sits: + Add source (named after its number, in capitals: SOURCE 12 when it lands at S12, or the next free number), + Add destination (always a real 1920×1080 destination at the end of the canvas, in every preset, Wire and the Excel; an I/O-only destination is made on Advanced page 1), + Add AUX (named with its number, or the next free one: AUX5 when AUX4 is taken; on in every preset, as the band’s +), + Add multiviewer, each one Undo step. Each + Add card is drawn as an empty outline of its section’s card (the picture box on the left for a source, on the right for the others), and a click anywhere on it, or Enter / Space, adds one; an empty section shows only its row of them. Numbers. Every source has an S number, every destination a D number, every AUX / DSM an A number, set by the show’s order (the order of this page; a PBP B or GFX B the app makes sits right under its A). Every card shows its number on every page, and the I/O Excel and the Look Book print it; it is not typed in. A name shows on its card as you typed it; a new one comes in capitals. Remove, at the right end of each section’s title, opens a picker of that section (Sources: the I/O-only sources; Destinations: the destinations and I/O-only destinations; AUX / DSM: the AUX / DSM outputs; Multiviewers: the multiviewers) and does what that card’s trash does; every card has its own trash. On the Simple patch, Add Source adds an I/O-only source: Wire, the Advanced patch and Video Presets (Simple’s content lists and Advanced’s All Sources) list it, and any preset can use it. Remove lists the I/O-only sources no preset uses; one a preset uses is a preset source. Add PBP A or GFX A anywhere and its B appears with it, as the backup row on an Advanced page.
Multiviewer (MV)
An operator-monitor reference. It is never drawn on the canvas or in presets; in Wire its card can be dragged onto the drawing. Its name is a box like any other row: type a new name and press Enter. In Simple its card shows the multiviewer picture it was given, one of four (a click on it shows the next), and so does its row on an Advanced page; it takes no uploaded picture or colour.
Advanced pages
A standalone patch builder, one patch per page. Every page has a Refresh column between Resolution and Notes (Custom… types your own rate, a positive number up to 3 decimals, then — Clear —, 23.98, 24, 25, 29.97, 30, 50, 59.94, 60, 120); on page 1 a show item’s rate is its own, so the I/O Excel (a Refresh column after Resolution on every tab), the Look Book (1920x1080 · 59.94) and the phone show it. The Notes cell shows the start of the note: click it (or Enter / Space) for a box under it with the whole note, Enter or a click outside saves, Escape puts it back. Tab walks every control of every row in reading order; Enter / Space opens a menu, the arrow keys move in it, Escape closes it. Page 1 opens as your show: the Simple rows under the show name; if Simple changes later you are offered a rebuild (not when only a Type changed that page 1 already shows). The last page is always a spare, × on a tab closes it, the copy icon duplicates it, double-click renames. The loop icon beside a source name pairs it with a backup source (one per primary); the backup row lines up under its primary and names ending in A and B pair on their own. A page with rows also appears in Wire’s I/O Tools as a tile with every input and output already labelled. Page 1 is the show: a source or destination you add there comes back to Simple as an I/O-only row, so Wire sees it too. A Type or note set on page 1 for a show item (typed, picked, — Clear —, Reset or Set for all) is that item’s own: the Look Book, both I/O Excel tabs and the phone show it, and a Type or note changed elsewhere (the phone’s I/O cards, the Video Presets Notes column) shows on page 1. The Type menu of a page-1 row that is a screen also offers Backdrop (after Stream): the screen becomes a backdrop and leaves the I/O Patch (it asks first, and says what happens). Pages 2 and up keep their own Types and notes. The rows page 1 copied from the show follow the show: a destination, AUX or source renamed in Video Presets is renamed on page 1 too; one removed in Video Presets stays on page 1 dimmed as “not in the show” with its notes, never comes back to Simple as an I/O-only row, is left out of the I/O Excel, and is a normal row again the moment the item is back. Rebuild from Simple or the row’s trash removes it. The backup icon is the same on every row: lit on a primary that has a backup, greyed on the backup itself. Every cable type and machine type carries its own icon from the Look Book icon pack, painted in the cable colour, so a row reads at a glance.
IP address
Set a row’s connector to NDI, ST-2110, Dante or Ethernet (on a Simple card, with a Set for all, on an Advanced row, on the phone’s I/O cards or on a Wire card) and its note gets the show’s next free IP address in the same Undo step: 192.168.0.1, then 192.168.0.5, .10, .15 … .250, then 192.168.1.1, .5 … One count for the whole show: an address already in any note, or typed in Wire’s Details, is skipped, and a Set for all gives each row its own. A note with text keeps it after the address (192.168.0.5 · Stage left); a note that already holds an IP address gets nothing. It is ordinary note text: change it or delete it like any note (on page 1 it is the item’s own note, so the Look Book and the Excel print it). Fiber and SFP add nothing, a change away from IP leaves the note as it is, and a show you open is never changed. Wire reads the first address in a note as that item’s IP.
Wire — Signal Flow
What it is
A diagram of the show’s signal flow — sources on the left, the router in the middle, destinations and AUX on the right, each a tile like its card on the left (its picture, name, resolution and cable type). It starts with every source cabled into the router and every destination and AUX out of it; click a preset on the right to light only what that look uses, or click a tile to read where it is used.
Simple vs Advanced
Simple starts as the whole show and is yours to edit, with Advanced’s cables: drag any card from the left onto it (it arrives cabled to the router’s next free row; a card that is on it already moves its tile), drag from a tile’s dot or a router row to cable it, drag a plugged end to move it (dropped on a point that has a cable, the two swap), select a cable and press Delete (or double-click it) to remove it, and press Delete or a tile’s × to take the tile off Simple (it stays in the show, drag its card back). One cable per tile and per router row. An item you add to the show later arrives cabled, unless you took it off Simple. The router is called Generic Router until you type a name in its title; its rows follow the cables; type an ID in a row’s ID cell (until you do, the cell shows the item’s IP). Advanced is a free-form builder with routers, switchers, converters and network switches (the I/O Tools menu) across multiple pages. A source tile on the canvas can carry up to six output points, each with its own cable type: select the tile and set them in Details. Page 1 opens as your show: a copy of the Simple drawing under the show name; if Simple’s tiles or cables change later you are offered a rebuild. The last page is always a spare, × on a tab closes it and the copy icon duplicates it. Cables are orthogonal: drag a plugged port to move that end of the cable to another port (Option-drag an output point to move the source end), select a cable for a handle on every straight run, double-click a handle to reset it. In Simple and Advanced alike a cable runs from an output to an input: let go on a point of the same kind (an output on an output, an input on an input) it does not attach, and a warning by the pointer says so for a few seconds, e.g. “PPT A OUT can not connect to OUT 3”.
Source thumbnails
Each source card carries a thumbnail tile (camera, slides, prompter…). The auto tile is the name on the card’s colour (it breaks only between words; a word too long is drawn smaller); a destination or AUX card has its picture on the right, and so has a destination or AUX tile in the drawing (Simple and Advanced, every page, a hand-made one too, and so the Wire sheets and the Look Book’s Wire page print it): its name, resolution and cable on the left, its cables meeting it where they always did; a source tile keeps its picture on the left. The shuffle icon picks another colour, a click on the tile uploads your own image, and the × on a hovered picture removes it. The cards on the left are the I/O Patch’s cards at Wire’s size, the same as on Video Presets › Advanced: the name box with its ▾ name list, Reset, the trash and the number too; the resolution ▾ reads Custom resolution…, — Clear —, the sizes used in this show, then the list. A change on any card shows on every page. Advanced’s hand-made cards (the + in a section’s title) are that card too, numbered C1, C2 … in their section (they are not in the I/O Patch); their Reset and trash ask first.
Tool headers
Every tool on the drawing, a router, a switcher, a converter, a network switch, a tile made from an I/O Patch page and Simple’s Generic Router, has a header with its pencil and name on the left, a picture on the right the size of a tile’s picture, half that on a converter (a tile made from an I/O Patch page shows a lock instead of the pencil: rename it on its page). A long name wraps onto a second line, and on every tool but a converter onto a third, breaking only between words (a word too long for the line breaks after its hyphens, or is drawn smaller; only a word too long even at the smallest size is split mid-word, at the largest size that keeps the other words whole); one longer still ends in … and shows in full when you point at it. Click the picture to upload your own image (a logo, a photo of the unit), and again to replace it at any time; the × on a hovered picture removes it; with the keyboard, Tab to the picture and press Enter. Drag the picture, or the bar, to move the tool. Without an image the picture shows the tool’s name. The whole header bar takes the colour of the image, or, without one, a colour of the tool’s own: picked at random when you add it; Simple’s Generic Router, and a tool from a show made before this header, show one worked out from the tool, the same every time. Its words turn white or black, whichever reads better. A router’s or switcher’s pencil changes its number of inputs and outputs; a converter’s, a switch’s and the Generic Router’s pencil puts you in its name. Advanced page 1 takes the Generic Router’s colour and picture when it is built. In a show saved before the pictures grew to this size, a tile right under a router, a switcher or a network switch moves down to make room the first time its page is drawn. The Wire sheets and the Look Book print the header, its colour and its picture.
Cable Type
Every Cable Type menu (the source, destination and AUX cards, the custom cards of Advanced, a source tile’s output points, converter and switch ports) reads like the I/O Patch Connector menu: Custom… first, — Clear — second, then the connectors. Custom… turns the button into a box right on the card: type your own connector (LEMO, opticalCON) and press Enter or click away. It has no colour code: its cable draws grey and the Cable Colour Code lists it as Custom. A connector typed on a source, destination or AUX card is that row’s connector in the I/O Patch, and the other way round.
IP address
An item’s IP is the first address in its I/O Patch note (a source’s IP typed in Details wins). On an Advanced router or switcher, an ID cell you have not typed in shows the IP of the source feeding that input or of the destination on that output, after the OUT n or BKP it showed there (OUT 1 · 192.168.0.1), drawn smaller when the column is narrow; a network switch’s port with no name shows the IP of what is cabled to it. Nothing is written into the show: it follows the note, prints on the Wire sheets and the Look Book’s Wire page, and what you type in the cell always wins (clear it and the IP is back). Details’ IP box of an NDI, ST-2110 or Dante source shows the address in its notes, or suggests the next free one: Enter uses it. A hand-made destination or AUX (Advanced) has the same box: its own IP, shown on its tile and in the cells and ports it is cabled to; an IP cable type picked on its card gives it the next free address.
Tile colours
A destination or AUX tile in the drawing shows the same colour as its card in the I/O Patch and in Wire (Simple and Advanced, every page; the Advanced Wire sheets and the Look Book’s Advanced Wire page print it). It works as a source’s colour does: the last of these wins: a picture you upload on its card (its main colour), a cable type you pick for it (on its card, on Advanced page 1, with a Set for all, on the phone or on its Wire card: that cable’s colour), the colour bar or the shuffle. The cable itself keeps the cable type’s own colour. Until then a destination is orange and an AUX yellow, and opening a show changes no colour. A hand-made destination or AUX tile shows its own card’s colour. The Simple drawing sheet prints every tile, sources too, in the sheet’s own colours.
Multiviewers
The Multiviewers list under AUX / DSM has a card for each multiviewer: its picture on the right (a click, or Enter / Space, shows the next of the four, as in the I/O Patch), its name, resolution and cable type. Drag a card onto the drawing to place it; nothing places it for you. In Advanced it is a tile you cable like a destination (from a switcher, router, converter or source), once per page: dragging it again moves that tile. In Simple it arrives cabled to the router’s next free output row, as any tile dropped there; dragging it again moves its tile. Select the tile and press Delete to take it off; deleting the multiviewer in the I/O Patch takes its tiles and cables off every page too. A placed tile prints on the Wire sheets and the Look Book’s Wire page.
Export & asset pack
Save the diagram as PDF / SVG / PNG on Letter, Tabloid, ANSI D / E, A1 or A0 sheets (pick the size in the export window); the page name prints large in the sheet’s upper-left corner, and orthogonal wires hop where they cross. The Asset Pack downloads every 1920×1080 thumbnail as one ZIP (sources / destinations / aux-dsm) — a ready-made image packet to hand your operators.
Preset tile — Modifiers ▾ menu (Blend & AOI)
Turn it on
Open the Modifiers ▾ menu at the top of a preset to switch on blend zones, area-of-interest, dead-space and free-positioning on the canvas. A switch shows on every preset, is not saved in the show and starts off each time the app opens. Fit Canvas in the same menu trims the preset and is one Undo step. Modifiers is not the Simple / Advanced switch of the page.
Make a blend
Drag one destination over its neighbour. The overlap shows as an orange hatch and the canvas reports the combined Blend Group resolution (e.g. 3240×1080).
No accidental overlaps
A destination never lands on top of another one without asking. A typed X / Y, size or rotation, a pasted or reset position, a corner-handle resize, a dead-space value, a resolution picked in I/O Patch or a destination put back into a preset that would overlap a neighbour all ask Create Blend Zone?, the same question a Free Position drop asks. Add to blend keeps it; Cancel puts everything back where it was. Opening a show never moves anything: old shows keep their blends.
Edit the overlap
Double-click the px number in the middle of the blend zone to type an exact overlap — it highlights for editing. A blended pair stays locked together and will not pull a third destination in on its own.
One combined screen
A blend is one combined screen: the group’s first destination in the destination list (D1 before D2) is the master. Its BG is one picture across the whole blended screen (the Blend Group’s W × H), and its layers go anywhere on it, across the blend zone too, on top of every destination and the hatch. A new layer starts in the middle of the whole blended screen. The other destinations stay separate outputs, but their row in the table reads Blended with the master, greyed: their own BG and layers are kept, hidden. Double-click the blend zone or its red % for the blend options: One combined screen switches it off (every destination shows its own BG and layers again) and on again, one Undo step. A blend made in this version starts on; a show from an earlier version opens exactly as it was, switch it on there. Destinations stacked at the same place are not a blend and stay as they are. Break Blend puts the master’s layers back inside it. While a destination is part of one combined screen its Rotation (Destination Properties) is off, greyed: switch One combined screen off or break the blend to rotate it.
Area of Interest
Select a destination and activate AOI to capture only part of it — drag the red box or type exact X / Y / W / H.
Dead space
A blue double-arrow between two destinations shows the pixel gap of unused canvas between them.
Video Presets — Advanced page (video)
Simple / Advanced
The pill at the top of Video Presets. Simple is the tile view. Advanced is the engineer page: the same preset tile in the centre, the cards on the left (All Sources, All Destinations, AUX / DSM), Properties on the right and the video timeline underneath.
The cards (left)
Three folding lists, as in Wire: All Sources (with its Images and Video tabs), All Destinations and AUX / DSM. Each card is the I/O Patch’s card at Wire’s size: the picture (click it to upload your own, the × on it removes it), the colour bar and the shuffle, the name (click it to rename; the ▾ is the name list), the resolution (type it, or pick it from its ▾), the cable type, Reset, the trash and the S1 / D1 / A1 number (set by the show’s order; it is not typed in). A change on a card is the same change on Wire, the I/O Patch, the Look Book and the Excel, one Undo step. The + Add card at the end of each list adds one at once (Source N, Destination N, AUX N, on in every preset); on the Video tab it imports video and picture files (MP4, MOV, WebM, images), which you can also drop on the list. A new source is named after its number, in capitals: SOURCE 12 when it lands at S12, or the next free number; its number follows the show’s order, as every number does, so it can change once a preset uses it. On the Video tab the + Add card is the outline of a file card. A new file is named after its file in capitals (WALK IN LOOP), gets a cable colour of its own, which it keeps on every page, and takes its number by the show’s order, like every source. A card on the Video tab is the source card with a video job in each slot: click its picture to play / pause the clip right there (only this page plays files), the frame rate and the length sit on the picture, the colour bar shows its sound (or NO AUDIO), the trash in the shuffle’s place removes the file from the show (it asks first, Undo brings it back), the name renames it everywhere (the stored file follows; the card shows the name as you type it), and the two boxes show its size and file type. A file missing from this app’s storage is a dashed card: click RELINK on its picture to pick the file again. A file is a source on every page: Wire, the I/O Patch and Simple’s lists show its cover. Drag a source card onto a layer chip, a layer row in Properties, a destination’s background (BG) or an AUX box. Every card shows a name as you typed it; a new name comes in capitals. A name breaks only between words; a word too long for its line is drawn smaller, down to 7 px; only a word too long even then breaks, after its _ or - first. The panel drags as wide as 360 px and no narrower than its cards.
Properties › Preset
Every preset as a card, a scaled clone of the tile. Click one to bring it to the centre. The AUX pills switch that preset’s outputs.
Properties › Layers
Pick a layer to edit it. Sections: Source, Media Info (file, path, resolution, frame rate, codecs, audio, bit depth), General (name, colour, notes, speed, loop), Position, Size, Opacity, Mask, Border, Shadow, Effects, and for pictures and clips Filters, Color, Source crop (fit and crop inside the source) and Transition (In / Out, fades). Each section has copy, paste and reset.
Timeline
Shows the picked layer’s video: a ruler with drag handles for In and Out, a strip of real frames, the audio waveform and a blue playhead. Click or drag anywhere on it to scrub.
Transport
Count-up from In · CLIP Stop / Play / Pause for the picked layer · 30 / 20 / 10 jump to the last seconds before Out · PRESET Stop / Play / Pause for every video in the preset together · Cover · count-down to Out. Picking another layer stops whatever was playing.
Audio level
The white line across the waveform is the level: bottom 0 %, middle 100 %, top 200 %. Drag it, double-click for 100 %. The L / R meters at both ends read the picked clip while it plays.
Cover
Uses the frame under the playhead as the picture Simple, the preset cards and the video’s source cards on Wire and the I/O Patch show for that video.
Display
Sends the preset that is open, clean, to a second window: drag that window to the other monitor and double-click it for full screen. It follows play, pause, scrub and the preset you pick; all control stays in this window. Reference playback only: H.264 and HEVC clips play, ProRes and HAP show their cover. Press Display again to close it.
Keys
Space play / pause · , and . step one frame · I and O mark In / Out · [ and ] previous / next preset · Escape closes whatever is open on top, then lets go of the picked layer, destination or AUX, then goes back to Simple. See the Keyboard tab.
DSM / AUX Outputs
Adding
Click + in the DSM toolbar below any preset. Each DSM has a name and a resolution (the same in every preset) and an on / off state per preset.
Name and content
Double-click a DSM box (or its pill in the band) to open its panel. A name typed in its Name box renames the DSM in every preset and on every page, as its card’s name box on the I/O Patch, Wire and Video Presets > Advanced does; an older show whose presets gave it names of their own opens with its main name in every preset. The content it carries is for that preset only, other presets are unaffected. Remove AUX Globally asks first, like the I/O Patch trash. There is no Type field in the panel: the DSM / AUX wording comes from the toolbar pill.
Content assignment
When a DSM is ON for a preset, assign a content type. This appears in the Excel export. Its box under the preset fills with that content’s colour (or its picture), however the content was set (this panel, a drop on the Advanced page, the table’s cell), on screen and in the Look Book.
Global label
The DSM / AUX pill in the toolbar sets the global default label. Individual presets can override it.
Destination Names
Global name
Typed in the Destination Combinations table on the first preset, on any other preset’s row, in its card’s name box (I/O Patch, Wire, Video Presets > Advanced), in Destination Properties’ Name box or in Edit Show Info: each renames the destination in every preset and on every page.
One name in every preset
An older show whose presets gave a destination (or an AUX / DSM) a name of their own opens with its main name in every preset, as part of opening: nothing to undo, nothing to save. Destination Properties has a Name box that renames the destination in every preset and on every page; its Remove Globally asks first, like the I/O Patch trash, and so does the ✕ on the destination’s first row of the Video Presets table.
Fallback
Every preset shows the destination’s one name, on screen, in the Look Book and in the Excel.
Save, Load & Export
.avlb file
The project file format (JSON, version 3). One file holds the whole show: destinations, presets, layers with their masks, effects and clip settings, AUX / DSM outputs, canvas size, show info, custom types, the I/O Patch (Simple and the Advanced pages) and the Wire pages with their thumbnails.
Autosave
Changes are saved automatically. The desktop app writes them into the show file itself, about every 30 seconds once the show has a file. The browser version keeps a draft in the browser: on the next open you are offered the draft or a fresh start. A restored draft comes back exactly as it was written, blend zones and free positions included, the same as opening a file; switch Blend Zones / Dead Space on in Modifiers to see them drawn. Until you save it, Open, New and the example shows ask before replacing it.
Unsaved indicator
The Save button turns gold while you have changes not yet written to a file.
↓ Excel
Exports the cue sheet as a styled .xlsx: a Cover tab, then one row per preset with a column per destination and per AUX / DSM, each cell listing the BG, the layers with their visible size and the AOI. Opens in Excel or Numbers.
↓ Look Book
Exports a print-ready visual. Opens browser print dialog, choose Save as PDF.
Send
Builds the Look Book and the Excel cue sheet from the show as it stands and adds the show file (.avlb). In the app a confirmation comes first and all three are attached to a new message, or, if the mail app will not open, they wait in Documents › AV Look Book › Outbox with the message text on your clipboard. In a browser it depends on the share sheet: where the browser hands files to the system share sheet the three go straight to it; where it does not, the three download to your Downloads folder instead and a pre-filled message opens naming them, for you to attach. Nothing leaves until you send that message yourself.
Report a bug
The bug button beside Help opens an email to AV Educate with the build and the system already filled in, and sends your show file with it so the bug can be seen on our side. In the app the file is attached for you, and if the mail app will not open the app says which folder it is in instead. In a browser nothing can be attached: the show file is downloaded to your Downloads folder and the message names it, for you to attach yourself. If you would rather not share the show, send the message without attaching the file, and delete the downloaded copy.
Preflight check
The cue-sheet Excel and the Look Book look the show over first: an error stops the Excel, a blank show name for one, while the Look Book takes those same findings as warnings and is never stopped, so a stale canvas size is said out loud before the book is built and you can still print it. The I/O Patch sheet runs its own check of the sources and destinations instead (missing connector type, missing resolution, a cable that cannot carry the resolution), which only ever warns, so it is never stopped either. Export Anyway carries on past warnings. Esc or Close goes back to the show.
New Show
Clears everything and opens Quick Setup. Warns if you have unsaved changes.
Quick Setup Wizard
Opening
Appears automatically on first load. Re-open with Project › New (Ctrl / Cmd + N). The pencil at the right end of the SHOW label, just above the Show name, opens it as Edit Show Info over the open show: name, Date Created, venue, destination names, resolutions and counts; presets and layers are kept. Update Show is one Undo step for the destinations and counts (the show name, Date Created and venue sit outside Undo, as in Wire › Project Info); Cancel or Escape changes nothing. While the window is open the page's shortcuts stand down (as under a dialog); the counters move one at a time from the show's real counts (the 24 / 8 / 12 limits belong to a fresh build); a blank Show name is refused; Update Show writes only what you changed.
Date Created, Show Dates
Date Created is the day the show was set up: type it, or press the calendar button in the box (or Alt / Option + ↓, or Space) and pick one day. Show Dates are the days of the show: type them, or pick the first day and then the last on the same calendar (the days between light up) and the box reads APRIL 8-10, 2026. Whatever you type by hand is kept exactly as typed. Both work the same in Wire › Project Info. The Excel cover prints the Show Dates; with Show Dates blank it prints CREATED and the Date Created.
Show Type
Corporate, Touring, Installation… typed by hand; the Excel cover prints it as SHOW TYPE. A show saved before this build keeps what it had in Show Format here.
Start from an example
Three finished shows ship inside the app: General Session, Awards Night and Town Hall. Open one from Quick Start (or the empty canvas), explore the presets, I/O and wiring, then Save As to make it yours. The same shows are on the website as training packets with their PDF and Excel.
Destination Names
Expand each destination row to give it a custom name before building. Falls back to Destination 01, 02… if blank.
Set default for all
When ON (blue), changing Destination 1's resolution cascades to all others (the row reading All Destinations: the first row, or the first screen row when the first is a backdrop). Turn OFF to set independently.
After setup
All destinations, one preset (GLOBAL PRESET 00), and any DSM outputs are created. Everything can be changed afterwards.
Pixel ↔ Feet Conversion
Reference standard
16 PPI — the most common LED tile is 192 pixels per foot, so that is where the conversion starts.
Default conversion
1 foot = 192 pixels (16 PPI × 12 inches). Adjust below if your venue uses LED panels with a different pixel density.
When it applies
Dead Space labels show FT values computed from the current PPI (visible when Modifiers ▾ Dead Space is on).
Adjust PPI
1 ft = 192 px

Terms used in live event production, show calling, and video switching, applicable across all platforms.
SHOW STRUCTURE
SHOW
The complete production, all screens, presets, and outputs for a single event or venue.
PRESET
A saved look, what content appears on which destination. Also called a cue, look, or snapshot.
TRANSITION
How the switcher moves from one preset to the next, cut, dissolve, or wipe.
CUE
An instruction to execute a preset. A show caller calls cues to the operator.
RUNDOWN
The ordered list of all cues/presets for a show.
DESTINATIONS & CANVAS
DESTINATION
A physical display or output, LED wall, projection screen, confidence monitor.
BACKDROP
A scenic piece in the row between the screens. It takes no video, is named BACKDROP, is sized in feet and inches (12' 6" × 8') and is left out of the canvas size, the I/O Patch and Wire. It has no destination number and shows only in the Video Presets.
CANVAS
The total pixel space across all screens.
RESOLUTION
The pixel dimensions of a destination, width × height (e.g. 1920×1080).
ASPECT RATIO
The proportional relationship between width and height (e.g. 16:9, 4:3).
PIXEL PITCH
Distance in mm between LED pixels. Smaller pitch = higher resolution.
LED WALL
A display made of tiled LED modules. Modular, scalable, very bright.
EDGE BLENDING
Softening the join between overlapping projector images for a seamless look.
NITS
Unit of brightness (cd/m²). Indoor LED: 800–1500 nits. Outdoor LED: 3000–6000 nits.
LAYERS & COMPOSITING
LAYER
A channel of content on a destination. Higher numbers sit on top.
PIP
Picture-In-Picture. A smaller layer positioned within a larger destination.
BACKGROUND / BKG
The base layer, fills the entire destination behind all other layers.
DSK
Downstream Key. A graphic keyed over the final output after compositing.
USK
Upstream Key. Applied before the final composite, used for camera keying.
CHROMA KEY
Removes a specific colour (green/blue screen) to create transparency.
LUMA KEY
Uses brightness levels to create transparency.
CROP
Trimming the edges of a layer without moving it.
OPACITY
How see-through a layer is, 100% opaque, 0% transparent.
AOI
Area of Interest. A cropped region of a destination used as a virtual output.
SEAMLESS SWITCHING
Transition between presets with no visible glitch or flash.
OUTPUTS & MONITORING
DSM
Discrete Secondary Monitor. Auxiliary output for confidence monitors or prompters.
AUX
Auxiliary output, used for monitors, record feeds, or overflow screens.
PROGRAMME / PGM
The main live output, what the audience sees.
PREVIEW / PVW
Pre-fade view, lets the operator see what happens next before committing.
MULTIVIEW
Single monitor showing multiple inputs and outputs in a grid.
RETURN FEED
Signal coming back from a remote location, streaming encoder, or broadcast truck.
CONFIDENCE MONITOR
Display visible only to the presenter, shows slides, notes, or timer.
IMAG
Image Magnification. Live camera feed shown on the main destination for large audiences.
SIGNAL & CONNECTIVITY
SDI
Serial Digital Interface. Professional broadcast cable for uncompressed digital video.
12G-SDI
Single-cable SDI carrying 4K video. Common in broadcast and live events.
HDMI
Consumer/prosumer digital connector. HDMI 2.0 supports 4K at 60fps.
NDI
Network Device Interface. Sends video over standard ethernet.
GENLOCK
Synchronising video signal timing to prevent tearing when switching sources.
FRAME RATE
Frames per second, 24p, 25p, 30p, 50p, 60p. All sources should match.
LATENCY
Delay between input and output. Critical for IMAG, sync with live action matters.
EDID
Info a display sends to the source about its capabilities. Switchers can emulate it.
HDR
High Dynamic Range. Wider brightness and colour range than standard SDR.
COLOUR SPACE
Range of colours a system can represent. Rec.709 = HD. Rec.2020 = 4K/HDR.
COLOUR & IMAGE
4:4:4 / 4:2:2 / 4:2:0
Chroma subsampling. 4:4:4 = full colour (best). 4:2:2 = broadcast. 4:2:0 = streaming.
10-BIT / 12-BIT
Bit depth, 10-bit = 1.07 billion colours, smooth gradients, no banding.
SDR
Standard Dynamic Range. Traditional brightness range up to ~100 nits.
HDR10
HDR format with static metadata, up to 10,000 nits. Common on LED walls.
HLG
Hybrid Log-Gamma. Live broadcast HDR, backward compatible with SDR displays.
PRODUCTION ROLES
SHOW CALLER
Calls cues live, directs the operator on when to transition.
TD / TECHNICAL DIRECTOR
Senior operator responsible for the switcher and signal flow.
PROJECT MANAGER / PM
Plans the production, builds the look book, defines destination layouts.
HIGH RES ENGINEER
Specialist operator for the high-resolution switcher.
MEDIA SERVER OP
Operates media server (Disguise, Green Hippo, Resolume), manages video playback.
TECHNICAL RIDER
Document specifying exactly what equipment and connections a performer needs.
PATCH SHEET / I/O LIST
Lists every input and output connection. The engineer counterpart to the look book.
CONTENT TYPE SHORTHAND
AUX
Auxiliary. A secondary output, feeds overflow screens, record decks, or monitoring. Also used as a DSM label.
BACKUP
Backup feed or source held in reserve, switched to if the primary source fails during the show.
BLANK
An empty / black layer with no content. Used to intentionally darken a destination or as a placeholder.
BUG
Channel bug or watermark, a small persistent logo or icon keyed over content, usually corner-positioned.
CAM
Camera. A live camera feed, handheld, jib, or static positioned at the event.
CHROMA KEY
Removes a specific colour (green or blue screen) to create transparency for compositing.
CLOCK
A live clock graphic, countdown timer or time-of-day, typically driven by the graphics system.
CONFIDENCE
Confidence Monitor. Display visible only to the presenter showing slides, notes, or a countdown timer.
DSK
Downstream Key. A graphic layer keyed over the final output after all compositing is complete.
FULL GFX
Full-frame graphic. A graphic that fills the entire destination, no camera or video behind it.
GFX
Graphics. Any text, title, animation, or designed visual element from the graphics system.
HANDYCAM
A small handheld or compact camera, often used for POV shots, audience, or backstage coverage.
IMAG
Image Magnification. Live camera feed shown on large destinations so the back of the audience can see the stage.
LOGO
A static or animated brand logo, corporate identity graphic held on a destination.
LOWER 3RD
Lower Third. A graphic keyed over the bottom third of the destination, typically name and title text.
LUMA KEY
Uses brightness levels (luminance) to create transparency, white areas become transparent.
MULTIVIEW
A single monitor output showing multiple inputs and outputs arranged in a grid for monitoring.
NOTES
Speaker notes or prompter text fed to a confidence monitor, not visible to the audience.
PGM
Programme. The main live output, the final composite signal going to the audience screens.
PLAYBACK
Pre-recorded video content played from a media server, laptop, or video playback system.
PREVIEW
Preview (PVW). Pre-fade view, lets the operator see the next source before taking it to programme.
PROMPTER
Teleprompter feed. Scrolling script text shown to the presenter, mirrored on a beam-splitter in front of the lens.
PTZ
Pan-Tilt-Zoom. A remotely operated robotic camera, controlled from the operator position without a camera operator on set.
RECORD
Record feed. A dedicated output routed to a recording device, captures the show for archive or streaming.
RETURN
Return feed. Signal coming back from a remote location, streaming platform, or broadcast truck.
SLIDES
Presentation slides, PowerPoint, Keynote, or similar, driven by a presenter clicker or operator.
STREAM
Live streaming output or input, feed going to or coming from a streaming encoder or CDN.
TEAMS
Microsoft Teams. Video conferencing feed shown on screen, either a remote presenter or a hybrid audience.
TEST
Test pattern or signal. Used for alignment, colour calibration, and signal verification during setup.
TICKER
Scrolling text strip, news ticker style running across the bottom of the screen with live updates.
TIMER
Countdown or count-up timer graphic, session timer, break timer, or show clock.
USK
Upstream Key. Applied before the final composite, typically used for camera keying over a background.
WEBEX
Cisco Webex. Video conferencing feed, remote presenter or hybrid delegate shown on screen.
ZOOM
Zoom Video Communications. Video conferencing feed, remote presenter or hybrid delegate shown on screen.

About AV Look Book

AV Look Book is a pre-production and planning tool designed for show callers, producers, and video engineers to streamline show development before arriving onsite. It serves as a centralized reference point that helps unify the entire visual workflow between LED, projection, and screen switcher teams.

Rather than handling live control or system programming, AV Look Book creates professional planning documents — including Excel and PDF outputs, that organize screen layouts, preset combinations, content references, and show flow into a clear visual guide for the whole production team.

The goal of AV Look Book is to provide a faster, more professional way to collaborate, communicate, and prepare complex visual shows with greater consistency and efficiency.

Each setting can be toggled on or off independently. Changes save automatically and persist across sessions.
UI Size
Scales the whole interface up or down. Helps with low vision or eye fatigue.
Reduce Motion
Disables transitions and animations. Helps users with vestibular disorders, attention conditions, or visual fatigue. When OFF, follows your OS preference automatically.
OFF
ON
High Contrast
Boosts text contrast above WCAG AAA. Brightens secondary text and dim labels for low-vision users.
OFF
ON
Custom Content Type Colors
Override the default colors for content types. Useful for users with color vision differences (deuteranopia, protanopia, tritanopia). Pick a color that you can clearly distinguish from the others.
Quick presets
One-click apply a palette optimized for a specific color vision difference. Replaces all 6 content type colors below.
